topic.title: the Microsoft outage
topic.claim: When Outlook and Teams went down, your work didn't stop. Only the proof that you were working did.
topic.moment: Friday morning, Teams won't load, Outlook spins, and after the first panic your day goes strangely quiet and you get the one real task done by lunch.

turn.actually: It stops the signals of work: the green dot, the instant reply, the cc to your boss. A lot of your day is spent making those signals.

topic.because: Your boss can't see your work, only your replies. So you stay green, reply in seconds and cc people, because that is what looks like work. Take the tools away and the signal goes, and the real work turns out to be smaller and quieter than the day felt.
topic.payoff: The outage took away the stage, not the work. Notice how your day felt without an audience.
topic.villain: an office that judges you by how fast you reply, not by what you finish
topic.behaviour: office workers spend much of the day replying, staying online and cc-ing to look busy
topic.mechanism: when work is invisible, people manage what is visible: replies and online status, so a tool outage removes the performance and leaves the actual work
topic.group: salaried office workers in India on Microsoft Teams and Outlook
topic.send_to: the colleague who spent today refreshing Teams to see if it's back
topic.why_now: Microsoft 365's global outage from late Thursday 12 Nov into Friday 13 Nov 2026 took down Outlook, Teams and Copilot
topic.news_peg: Microsoft 365 global outage, 12-13 November 2026: Outlook, Teams and Copilot down for over 12 hours

sources.fact: A Microsoft 365 outage that began Thursday 12 November 2026 at 1:26 PM ET (11:56 PM IST) disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot, OneDrive and other Microsoft services worldwide.

sources.excerpt: Microsoft outage affects users worldwide, impacting Teams, Outlook and Copilot | still ongoing as of 5:06pm AEDT Friday 13 November | partial recovery that was not sustained | no indication this is a cyber attack | reverting a recent network configuration change

_ledger.text:
[cover] If one company can switch off your workday, you don't have a job.
You have a login.
 

[slide 1] If one company can switch off your workday, you don't have a job.
You have a login.

[slide 2] Around midnight on Thursday, Outlook, Teams and Copilot went down.
Twelve hours later your mission-critical work was still waiting for someone else's servers to come back.

[slide 3] We love calling India the world's back office.
Last night the back office couldn't open its own email.

[slide 4] Your company calls it a cloud-first strategy.
Say it plainly. We rent everything, and the landlord holds the keys.

[slide 5] India refused to let one company own UPI.
Then offices handed one company their email, their meetings and their files, and called it digital transformation.

[slide 6] Your IT team couldn't fix it. Your CEO couldn't escalate it.
Your senior title meant nothing. Today everyone had the same job: refresh.

[slide 7] Tomorrow it all comes back and nobody changes a thing.
That's the real outage.

[end card] 
Send this to the colleague who called today a productive break.

[caption] The Microsoft outage was a reality check: if one company can switch off your workday, you're only renting it.

The world's back office spent the morning refreshing a status page.

Send this to the colleague who called today a productive break.

[alt text] A text post arguing that the Microsoft outage exposed how Indian offices rent their entire workday from one company.

2d7188d7fef8ecafc8be2238dd9f19a34f363ac2.actual_mechanism: Outlook, Teams and Copilot are Microsoft 365 services Microsoft runs on its own Azure cloud (physical datacenters), and the Nov 12-13, 2026 incident began with an Exchange Online failure (~16:17 UTC Nov 12) that cascaded across Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and even third-party AI tools using M365 connectors, hitting 74 countries within an hour. The cloud market is genuinely concentrated: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud together hold roughly two-thirds (~67%) of global cloud infrastructure, so unrelated firms and direct competitors do commonly depend on the same few providers, and a single provider's failure takes down everyone renting from it simultaneously, everywhere.

Around midnight on Thursday, Outlook, Teams and Copilot went down.
Twelve hours later your mission-critical work was still waiting for someone else's servers to come back.
We love calling India the world's back office.
Last night the back office couldn't open its own email.
Your company calls it a cloud-first strategy.
Say it plainly. We rent everything, and the landlord holds the keys.
India refused to let one company own UPI.
Then offices handed one company their email, their meetings and their files, and called it digital transformation.
Your IT team couldn't fix it. Your CEO couldn't escalate it.
Your senior title meant nothing. Today everyone had the same job: refresh.
Tomorrow it all comes back and nobody changes a thing.

mechanism.actual_mechanism: Outlook, Teams and Copilot are Microsoft 365 services Microsoft runs on its own Azure cloud (physical datacenters), and the Nov 12-13, 2026 incident began with an Exchange Online failure (~16:17 UTC Nov 12) that cascaded across Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and even third-party AI tools using M365 connectors, hitting 74 countries within an hour. The cloud market is genuinely concentrated: AWS, Azure and Google Cloud together hold roughly two-thirds (~67%) of global cloud infrastructure, so unrelated firms and direct competitors do commonly depend on the same few providers, and a single provider's failure takes down everyone renting from it simultaneously, everywhere.

sources.quote: Microsoft is investigating a widespread outage affecting multiple Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams, and Copilot... customers may be unable to connect to multiple services, including Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot, and Microsoft Defender XDR.

Amazon's market share in the worldwide cloud infrastructure market was 28 percent... ahead of Microsoft's Azure platform at 21 percent and Google Cloud at 14 percent; the top three vendors' combined share is roughly two-thirds of the market.
